accuracy.evidence: Checked for the Arctic tundra lesson against the NPS Arctic nature and science page (tundra from a Finnish word for a treeless plain; growing season 50 to 60 days; permafrost under the tundra; the active layer thaws in summer and saturated ground forms bogs and ponds), the UNEP atlas tundra chapter (summer 3 to 12 °C, little precipitation, lakes, ponds and bogs because the topsoil sits on permafrost), the USDA Forest Service NRS-80 tundra chapter (surface layers thaw each summer usually to less than 1 m; snowpack usually lasts 9 months or more; permafrost restricts deep roots and keeps the thawed layer waterlogged), NSIDC frozen-ground definition (at or below 0 °C for two or more years), the National Wildlife Federation Arctic environment notes (no trees because roots cannot spread in permafrost and wind; plants keep low), and Ambio 2011 (snow covers Arctic land 8 to 10 months). Caribou cratering for lichen, lemmings living under the snow, musk ox long guard hair and dense underwool, snowy owls' feathered feet and lemming diet, Arctic poppy flowers tracking the sun, lichen as fungus plus alga, and penguins being Southern Hemisphere only all match the cited species notes. Every numeric item was evaluated at its range corners (10+5 to 30+20 cm, 12-7 to 12-10 months, 100-30 to 100-60 cm, 365-50 to 365-60 days).

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the common naive ideas about the tundra: that it is ice all year (challenge 'Covered in ice all year', practice m7), that permafrost means the whole ground is frozen even in summer (prediction 'Yes, it all thaws' is disproved when the pole slides 50 cm in summer; challenge 'All of it, right down' and 'None of it'), that meltwater soaks deep down (prediction and the tap on the top layer is refused), that trees are missing for lack of water (prediction option 'There is no water', challenge slip 'water'), that penguins live in the Arctic (prediction, sort scene and challenge), and that lemmings fly south or dig into permafrost.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagtundra is built on the tundra's own mechanism: a soil cross-section with a 0 to 150 cm scale where a draggable pole stops at the 50 cm permafrost table in summer and will not enter in winter, snow heaps melted by dragging the sun whose meltwater runs down and pools on the frozen layer before the learner taps the layer that blocks it, planting where a tall pine is refused with its roots drawn hitting the ice, an animal sort that rejects penguin, camel and monkey, and a winter-trick match. It is not 652 flagarcant (Arctic versus Antarctic places), 936 midnight sun, 645 polar animals or 729 polar bears; the 6-token shingle gate reports no flag lab above 30%.

lab_teaches.evidence: The ideas are found by doing: the pole physically stops at 50 cm in summer and at 0 cm in winter, so 'only the top thaws' is discovered before it is stated; the meltwater lines visibly stop at the dashed permafrost line and spread into ponds, so the boggy summer follows; the pine bounces with roots meeting the ice, so 'no trees' has a cause; sorting and matching then tie each animal to a winter adaptation. Each finished step prints the rule (LEARNT) and compares it with the learner's prediction.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions, each with a tempting wrong option that the lab then disproves: 'Yes, it all thaws' (the pole stops at 50 cm), 'It sinks deep down' (the water stops and ponds), 'There is no water' (the bog is full of water, yet the tree is refused for its roots), and 'Yes' to penguins on the Arctic tundra (the sort refuses it with the far-south reason). The reveal line names the right answer after the task.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven challenge questions; each wrong option carries its own named slip: snow versus permafrost, sea ice versus frozen ground, all thaws, none thaws, rain versus trapped meltwater, no water, trees eaten, tundra animals mistaken for the odd one out, lemmings flying south, digging into permafrost, and ice all year. Clicked through all seven in a Playwright run; each shows the matching message and a Next button.

readability.evidence: Kid text FK grade 2.5 (family target 5.0) with short sentences and concrete words (stick, frozen, ponds, moss); permafrost is explained at first use. Adult text FK 9.7 (target 10) gives the definition, active layer depth, growing season, plant list and named mistakes. Canvas text is one short heading per scene, labelled layers (Thaws in summer, Frozen in winter, Top layer, Permafrost) and short cards.

no_filler.evidence: Kid paragraphs: what and where the tundra is; permafrost, the thawed top and why water ponds; what grows and why trees cannot; who lives there and the penguin slip. Adult paragraphs: where it is, the name and curriculum fit; permafrost, active layer, drainage, season length and plant list; named mistakes; what the lab does. The content gate finds no filler phrase and no explanation above 12% overlap.

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px phone screenshots in light and dark for every scene mid-task and finished: the Summer and Winter cards and the pole handle are large tap targets, the cm scale and layer labels are readable, the three snow heaps and the sun are spaced across the width with labelled layers, the six plant cards sit in a 3-column grid with planted names staggered so they do not overlap, animal cards are in 2 columns above two bins, and trick cards span the width above a 2 by 2 animal grid. Nothing is clipped.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button twin: Summer, Winter and 'Push the pole down', 'Melt snow heap 1-3', 'Top layer (thaws in summer)' and 'Permafrost (frozen all year)', 'Plant: Moss' style buttons, 'Caribou → tundra' and '→ elsewhere' buttons, and per-animal trick buttons. The canvas aria-label carries each scene description and every piece of feedback (pole depth, melt, plant facts); challenge feedback is a role=status live region; ✓ and ✗ mark state as well as colour; walk.cjs axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) is clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
